summary: A light on a rock at the approach to New Bedford Harbor, first lit in 1828; a fog trumpet, a wooden house and the 1938 hurricane, then a skeleton tower with a flashing green light.

structures.note: First station, lantern on the roof (D'Entremont).

structures.type: square wooden tower on wood-frame dwelling
structures.note: USLHS gives 1889 for the tower establishment; D'Entremont gives 1890 for the dwelling.

access.note: USLHS record: not open to the public.

events.note: First lit 19 October 1828 (D'Entremont); the USLHS record gives 1828 as the year established.
New wood-frame dwelling, 26 by 34 feet, with a square wooden tower attached (USLHS gives 1889 for the tower).
Changed on 22 December 1893 from fixed white to fixed white with a fixed red sector covering Mishaum Ledge.
Daboll trumpet operated by an oil steam engine, established 12 October 1897.
Cable laid connecting the station to the mainland telephone line.
Engine house enlarged, brick oil house built, steam oil engines replaced by 4-horsepower Hornsby-Akroyd oil engines.
Keeper J. E. Rogers and assistant C. E. Ellis towed the disabled motor boat Nistia, six men aboard, to shore (16 November 1919; the Commissioner's fiscal 1920 table lists it).
Power boat Kyra, five men aboard, drifted onto Dumpling Rock on 31 July; keeper helped pull it off and anchor it.
Extensive damage in the September 1938 hurricane.
Steel skeletal tower, per the USLHS record. D'Entremont gives 1942 for the removal of the house and the erection of the skeleton tower.
House removed and skeleton tower with flashing green light erected (D'Entremont).

corrections.why: The USLHS record places the light at Dartmouth, off New Bedford Harbor (Dartmouth is in Bristol County); the Barnstable entry seems to come from Wikipedia's county category, not from a source on the station.

corrections.proposed: tower, steel skeletal, built 1940 (USLHS) or 1942 (D'Entremont); the wooden tower dates from 1889-1890 and was removed
corrections.why: The 1942 structure is the steel skeleton tower; the wood material belongs to the earlier tower that the USLHS record says was damaged in the 1938 hurricane.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1828 date is the first stone station, first lit 19 October 1828; the 1942 (or 1940) date is the skeleton tower that replaced the wooden house. Both dates are for different structures.

Fixed white from 1828 until 22 December 1893, when a red sector covering Mishaum Ledge was added; the present light is a flashing green (D'Entremont). The record's conflicting entries describe different periods.

USLHS gives 1916-1933 and D'Entremont 1927-1933. The Commissioner's fiscal 1920 table and the Bulletin place Rogers at the station in November 1919 and July 1921, which fits the Archive's earlier start. The story states the disagreement.

USLHS gives the original optic as fifth-order Fresnel without a date; D'Entremont gives a fourth-order lens in the lantern of the 1890 tower. The records may describe different periods, so they are not treated as a direct conflict.

notes_for_editor: Dates: the Archive's roster is cited for every keeper line. The 1894 Board report entry (Dec 1893 change) sits in the fiscal year ended June 30, 1894; the 1896 volume carries a later note that the trumpet was established on October 12, 1897. Scan pages are given; printed page numbers were not confirmed. Conflicts not settled: (1) status: USLHS record says not an active aid; D'Entremont says the automatic light remains active; the station record says inactive. (2) first tower date 1889 (USLHS) vs 1890 dwelling (D'Entremont). (3) lens: fifth order (USLHS) vs fourth order in the 1890 lantern (D'Entremont). (4) replacement 1940 (USLHS) vs 1942 (D'Entremont, and the Wikipedia infobox, not cited). Wikipedia gives 1829 for the first stone light and Barnstable County; not used as a source. The USCG Historian's article on Dumpling Rocks Light could not be read: the Wayback capture returned only the banner page; it should be checked. Roster name variants: Maynard F. Rush (1896-1909 in USLHS, 1896-1908 in D'Entremont); John E. Rogers (1916-1933 in USLHS, 1927-1933 in D'Entremont; the Board and Commissioner lists confirm Rogers as keeper in 1920-1922); Henry J. Fontneau (USLHS) is spelled Fontineau by D'Entremont. The roster keeps the USLHS spelling and years. OCR: the Bulletin for 1920 (PDF page 3) is badly interleaved; 'O. E. Ellis' is read as C. E. Ellis by matching the 1918-1923 index and the 1920 Commissioner list; the vessel's name is not legible and is left out. The 1921 Kyra passage in the Bulletin is interleaved; the Commissioner's 1922 page (scan 752) carries the detail. The 1938 Bulletin's Massachusetts sentence is read across two OCR lines. Other stations: D'Entremont says Octave Ponsart later served at Butler Flats, Cuttyhunk and West Chop, but gives no years, so no other_stations entries were added. The Lighthouse Board reports from before 1891 are not in the local corpus; the 1828 to 1890 history rests on D'Entremont and the USLHS record. Newspaper search (Chronicling America, Massachusetts, 1880-1942) gave no usable hit. Accessed dates use the system date, 2026-10-28. Checker notes (2026-10-27): (1) The Nistia tow is dated 16 November 1919, not 1920. The Bulletin's 1920 volume issues run January to May 1920 and list October to December 1919 assistance in that same issue; the Commissioner's fiscal 1920 table (printed page 56, scan 554, July 1919 to June 1920) also lists Rogers and Ellis with the motor boat Nistia, six men aboard. The year is inferred from that issue chronology and the table, not stated in the Bulletin line. (2) The Commissioner's fiscal 1920 table has OCR 'Pumpling Rock' and was read on the page image as Dumpling Rock. (3) The Bulletin 1921 Kyra passage (printed page 196) was read on the page image: the Department commended John E. Rogers, keeper, for assistance rendered on July 31. (4) The 1920 Bulletin printed page 111 was read on the page image (Nistia, six men aboard). (5) The USLHS record flags 'Existing: No' for the light station, while the skeleton tower stands and the Archive's own disposition says it was replaced in 1940; the story does not resolve this. (6) The 1889 tower date and the 1890 dwelling date are different structures in the two sources and are left as stated. (7) The 1828 to 1890 history rests on D'Entremont and the USLHS record, since the pre-1891 Board reports are not in the local corpus; the Board's 1894 to 1901 entries were checked on the scan pages cited.
